vignette:
Alex is a man accustomed to control. As a combat pilot, his life is a study in precision, a world of checklists, physics, and split-second decisions where mastery of self and machine is the only thing that matters. For ten years, that world was his sanctuary. But the man who presented for therapy six months after an incident during shore leave was a stranger to that controlled self. The trauma was not from combat, but from a profound betrayal. During a night out with his squadron, a fellow officer he considered a close friend assaulted him in his hotel room. The attack was sudden, disorienting, and shattered Alex's belief in the very structure of his world-in loyalty, safety, and his own ability to judge character.

In the weeks that followed, Alex tried to bury the event, treating it like a mechanical failure to be troubleshot and forgotten. But the system wouldn't reset. His mind, once a finely tuned instrument, now felt like a faulty alarm. The conviction that he had been betrayed by someone he trusted metastasized into a global loss of faith; he now saw potential threats in everyone. This belief made him acutely sensitive to his surroundings, and he began to perceive danger in the most innocuous situations. A stranger holding his gaze for a moment too long on the street, or a colleague shifting their weight unexpectedly behind him at the base, became a trigger that flooded his system with adrenaline. These moments, born from his deep-seated mistrust, left him feeling constantly on guard, his body braced for an impact he couldn't see coming.

This state of perpetual threat has become his new normal. At home, the place he once retreated to for quiet and solitude, he feels as exposed as if he were in hostile territory. He startles violently at the ordinary sounds of his apartment building-the hum of the elevator, a neighbor's door closing down the hall. Each noise is a potential intrusion, and he finds himself monitoring every creak and groan of the building, listening for footsteps that aren't there. The exhaustion of this constant vigilance is immense, and it feeds a vicious cycle of self-recrimination. He sees his inability to relax, his jumpiness, as undeniable proof of his own weakness. 'I am a lousy coper,' the thought runs on a loop in his mind. A man who flies at Mach 2, who trusts his life to a complex machine, now feels broken by the sound of his own refrigerator kicking on. This deep sense of personal failure only reinforces his belief that he is fundamentally unsafe and alone.

The hypervigilance has, in turn, warped his perception further. Because he is always scanning for danger, he finds it everywhere. His state of high alert primes him to notice things he previously would have ignored, creating its own triggers. An unpredictable change in traffic patterns on his drive to the base can now spark a sense of panic, his mind and body reacting as if to a direct, personal threat. The residue of nightmares clings to him long after he wakes, the feeling of dread poisoning his mornings and making the world outside his door seem menacing and fraught with peril. He has come to believe that people are fundamentally untrustworthy, and this core belief now acts as a lens, filtering all his interactions and making him scan constantly for signs of suspicious behaviour.

His life has shrunk accordingly. He avoids squadron social events, unable to bear the unpredictability of a crowded room. His performance has suffered; his commanding officer noted his fatigue and distraction during a recent flight review, a conversation that felt like a final confirmation of his failure. It was the fear of being grounded, of losing the one part of his identity he still clung to, that finally propelled him to seek help. Alex sits in the therapy room, a coiled spring of a man, terrified that he is permanently broken, but holding onto a desperate hope that he might one day learn to feel safe in his own skin again, to trust the world-and himself-enough to finally stand down from his post.
